reading.rtitle: Welcome to Your First Week -- Orientation Guide for Incoming Residents
paras: THE FIRST DAY. Please show up at the residents' office at seven o'clock on Monday with two forms of identification. You will receive your badge and your login for the electronic record. If your credentialing has not come through yet, do not put off telling us: the program coordinator will look into it the same morning, and a delay is never held against a new resident.

THE SCHEDULE. Interns on the dermatology service take on four clinic sessions a week, plus one procedure session. It is easy to fall behind on notes in the first month, when the record system is new. Residents who catch up on their notes at the end of each day, rather than at the weekend, report far less stress by October.

ASKING FOR HELP. Nobody expects you to know everything in July. If you come across a term or a protocol you do not recognize, look it up in the online manual first. If it is not there, bring it up at the afternoon huddle: somebody else almost certainly has the same question. Attendings are asked to point out errors privately and in the same session, never in front of patients.

LIFE OUTSIDE THE HOSPITAL. International graduates tell us that the hardest thing to deal with in the first month is not the medicine but the paperwork. Most say they could get by in clinic with the English they arrived with, but not on the phone with an insurance company. The residents' office keeps a list of who to call for what. Ask for it on Monday.
reading.source: Teaching guide written for this lesson in the format American residency programs use. The procedures and the vocabulary are the target; it is not the guide of any real program.

listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome. I am the chief resident, and I am going to tell you the three things I wish somebody had told me in my first week. First, show up early, but do not try to look like you know everything. You will come across things you have never seen, and nobody expects otherwise. Look them up, and if you cannot find them, bring them up at the afternoon huddle. The worst thing you can do is nod and say nothing. Second, notes. Every single year, somebody falls behind on notes in the first month, and every single year it is the same person who said I will catch up at the weekend. You will not. Catch up every evening before you go home, even if it is only twenty minutes. Third, when an attending points something out, they are not grading you. They are teaching you. Write it down and deal with it the same day. And if there is a problem with your badge, your login or your paperwork, do not put it off. Come to the office. We will look into it. That is literally what we are here for.

My first week as a resident in the United States, I made one decision that saved me and one that nearly sank me. The bad one first. I thought I could get by without asking questions. My English was good enough for patients, I told myself, and I did not want to look slow. So when I came across an abbreviation I did not know, I guessed. On the Wednesday, an attending pointed out, very politely, that I had guessed wrong in three notes. Nothing bad had happened to anybody, but I went home that night feeling terrible. The good decision came the next morning. I took a small notebook and wrote down every term I did not know, and I looked them up on my break. Twenty, thirty a day at first. By the end of the month it was five. And I started bringing things up at the huddle instead of pretending. The attending who had pointed out my mistake told me later that it was the questions that convinced her I was going to be fine. So my advice is simple. Do not put off the questions. Nobody will think less of you for asking.
